title: Research
Research
text:
Microbes in coral reef sediments
Reef sediments are a hotspot of nutrient cycling but remain largely unexplored at genome level. From 191 sediment metagenomes collected at 48 sites across the Great Barrier Reef, I recovered 2,698 metagenome-assembled genomes (1,201 species), 98% of which have no species-level representative in reference databases. Compared with co-located seawater, sediment microbes have larger, GC-rich genomes and greater metabolic versatility, including anaerobic respiration, nitrogen fixation, hydrogen metabolism and novel biosynthetic gene clusters.
At Pelorus Island and Davies Reef, habitat type (front reef, back reef and lagoon) structures prokaryotic communities more than reef location, with metabolically flexible habitat generalists dominating. Sediment viruses, in contrast, are highly novel, local, and structured by reef location.

title: About me
text:
Hello! I am Hisatake (Take) Ishida, a microbial genomicist at the Australian Centre for Ecogenomics (ACE), School of Chemistry and Molecular Biosciences, The University of Queensland.
I have submitted my PhD thesis, supervised by Associate Professor Cheong Xin Chan and Professor Cynthia Riginos. I now work as a senior research technician at ACE and as a Learning Design Officer at UQ, where I develop software tools for teaching in undergraduate courses, while finalising manuscripts from my PhD.

title: About me
text:
PhD research
Ecology, Evolution, and the Environment: tackling “challenging” microbes of coral reefs using hologenomics and metagenomics
Coral reefs depend on microbes in seawater, sediments and the tissues of reef organisms. Some of these microbes are “challenging”: hard to culture, hard to sample, or hidden in data dominated by other organisms. My PhD used genome-scale data taken directly from the environment to study two such groups:

Endosymbiotic dinoflagellates (family Symbiodiniaceae) in reef-building corals. Using the microbial fraction of 4,013 coral hologenomes, I assessed symbiont diversity across the Indo-Pacific, showed how host genetics and the environment shape symbiont communities, and recovered 32 genomes of Cladocopium directly from coral tissue (in hospite).
Free-living prokaryotes and viruses in coral reef sediments of the Great Barrier Reef. I recovered 2,698 metagenome-assembled genomes representing 1,201 species, 98% of which have no species-level reference, and showed how reef habitat structures sediment communities and their metabolic potential.
